title: NavBind: Diagnosing Instruction-Action Binding at Route Forks in Navigation VLAs

paper.title: NavBind : Diagnosing Instruction-Action Binding at Route Forks in Navigation VLAs
paper.abstract:
Abstract Vision-language-action (VLA) navigation models translate visual observations and instructions into actions.
Navigation success assesses whether an agent reaches the goal.
However, reaching the goal successfully does not establish whether the model genuinely follows the instructions or relies on visual cues or navigation history.
We introduce NavBind to diagnose instruction-action binding: whether changing the instruction influences the probabilistic distribution of the actions, with the navigation context fixed.
We construct 3,252 route-fork contexts by recombining route-aligned instruction segments from R2R-CE and RxR-CE.
Each context pairs full instructions that share the description of the route already traveled but specify different branches.
Both are evaluated under the same agent state and navigation history.
We compare generated local action sequences, the likelihoods of fixed reference action sequences under both instructions, and changes in visual attention and attribution.
Across the evaluated models, higher reported navigation success does not imply that the model more faithfully follows the instructions.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1: Does the action follow the instruction? NavBind pairs one fixed navigation history H H with two full instructions P + S A P+S_{A} and P + S B P+S_{B} . The shared prefix P P describes the completed route, and the remaining suffixes S A S_{A} and S B S_{B} specify different executable branches. This example contrasts turning left with going up the stairs. We jointly examine generated action-sequence changes, fixed-target action likelihood, visual attention, and attribution for each instruction’s corresponding reference actions. In vision-and-language navigation in continuous environments (VLN-CE) ( Krantz et al., 2020 ) , vision-language-action (VLA) models ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) map visual observations and instructions to actions. Success rate measures whether an agent reaches the goal but does not establish whether it follows the instruction. Route-fidelity metrics ( Jain et al., 2019 ) assess the similarity between the generated trajectory and the ground-truth trajectory, providing an indirect measure of instruction following. However, these metrics still cannot establish whether the model genuinely follows the instructions , as it may instead rely on visual cues or navigation history alone. Language interventions, i.e., changing the language instruction and observing how the local actions or navigation performance change, provide a more direct test of language dependence. NavTrust ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) and Contrast Sets ( Anwar et al., 2025 ) rephrase instructions and assess changes in navigation performance. However, these tests keep the intended navigation behaviour unchanged. R2RIE-CE ( Taioli et al., 2024 ) modifies instructions by injecting direction, object, and room errors. However, it neither ensures that the modified instructions describe feasible routes nor provides reference actions corresponding to them. Without matching reference trajectories for the modified instructions, a behavioural change alone does not show that the model followed them. We therefore ask not merely whether the model’s behaviour changes, but whether changing the instruction to describe another feasible route makes the model more likely to choose the corresponding actions . We keep the agent’s state, navigation history, and completed instruction prefix fixed. In Figure 1 , both turning left and continuing up the stairs are feasible, and the remaining instruction specifies which branch to take. We use instruction-action binding to describe the requirement that the model assigns higher probability to the actions required by the instruction. We introduce NavBind , a controlled diagnostic built through cross-route recombination of route-instruction examples drawn from R2R-CE and RxR-CE. Using fine-grained route-language alignments, we retain one example’s completed instruction prefix and combine it with either its original suffix or a compatible suffix from another route. The resulting full-instruction pairs specify different executable branches under the same replayed history and agent state, yielding 3,252 contexts with reference action sequences for both branches. Within each fixed context, we first ask: does changing the instruction change the action sequence the model generates? We then ask: does the model assign higher probability to the actions for a branch when instructed to take that branch rather than the other? We test this by comparing the likelihood of each reference action sequence under the two instructions. This comparison can reveal changes in action preference even when the generated sequence stays the same. Finally, we examine the visual response: do attention heatmaps and gradient-based attribution heatmaps highlight different image regions under the two instructions? We evaluate four navigation VLAs on NavBind : Uni-NaVid ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) , StreamVLN ( Wei et al., 2025 ) , JanusVLN ( Zeng et al., 2026 ) , and FutureNav ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) . We find that higher reported navigation success does not imply that the model more faithfully follows the instructions. (Table 1 ). It also shows that models respond more strongly when the instructions contrast opposite turns than when they contrast forward movement with a turn. Our contributions are: • We construct NavBind by recombining instruction segments across routes into full instructions for two feasible branches. Each pair preserves the agent state, history, and completed instruction prefix, and provides reference action sequences for both branches. • We diagnose instruction-action binding using generated sequences to measure output changes, fixed-target likelihoods to assess preferences for the instructed actions, and attention and gradient-based attribution heatmaps to track spatial changes. • We show that higher reported navigation success does not imply that the model more faithfully follows the instructions. This supports evaluating how language affects local decisions alongside navigation success.

sections.heading: Instruction fidelity beyond success.
sections.text: Goal completion can obscure whether an agent followed the described route. Stay on the Path introduced CLS and longer R4R routes ( Jain et al., 2019 ) , while LAW extended language-aligned supervision and evaluation to VLN-CE ( Raychaudhuri et al., 2021 ) . Modality ablations further showed that R2R agents could rely strongly on graph structure ( Hu et al., 2019 ) . These works motivate language-specific evaluation through task metrics, supervision, and modality ablations.

sections.heading: Language interventions in VLN.
sections.text: Early diagnostics mask object, direction, and numerical cues ( Zhu et al., 2022 ) and swap directional tokens ( Hahn et al., 2023 ) . Skill-focused evaluations append atomic instructions to truncated RxR episodes ( Yang et al., 2023 ) and construct human-refined atomic instructions, including same-start left/right pairs ( Wang et al., 2024 ) . These studies evaluate agents on discrete navigation graphs and their action tests cannot be directly applied to navigation VLAs that execute low-level actions. In VLN-CE, NavTrust evaluates whether agents maintain navigation performance under instruction corruption and stylistic variation ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) . Contrast Sets tests instruction rephrasing with unchanged navigation goals on a physical robot ( Anwar et al., 2025 ) . However, these tests keep the intended navigation behaviour unchanged. R2RIE-CE injects direction, object, and room errors into instructions to study error detection and localization ( Taioli et al., 2024 ) . The modified instructions are not paired with matching reference trajectories. However, it neither ensures that the modified instructions describe feasible routes nor provides reference actions corresponding to them. Without matching reference trajectories for the modified instructions, a behavioural change alone does not show that the model followed them. CAST pairs generated alternative instructions with short action branches for counterfactual training ( Glossop et al., 2026 ) , but the intended action behaviour only include a short horizon rather than a long horizon. NavBind constructs full-instruction pairs for long-horizon navigation by recombining original route-aligned instruction spans across source routes. The pairs specify different executable branches under the same agent state, navigation history, and completed instruction prefix. Scoring both reference action sequences under both instructions tests whether the model’s local action preferences shift toward the instructed branch.

sections.heading: 2.2 Language-Action Coupling in VLAs
sections.text: Recent work examines whether language and other multimodal signals influence VLA action generation. VLA-Trace connects representation similarity, attention-path knockouts, and rollout-level behavioural probes ( Shi et al., 2026 ) , while Häon et al. (2025) identify semantic activation directions and intervene on them to steer actions. Zhang et al. (2026b) diagnose linguistic blindness in manipulation VLAs using contradictory instructions and recalibrate attention at inference time, while Zhan et al. (2026) study robustness to linguistic perturbations and strengthen language guidance through residual steering. These studies establish that language and internal pathways can affect VLA actions, but their evaluations center on manipulation and often combine diagnosis with model modification. NavBind tests instruction-action binding in frozen navigation VLAs: two valid route instructions share the same history but specify different executable branches. We align behaviour with fixed-target likelihood and visual attribution.

sections.heading: 3.1 VLN-CE
sections.text: In vision-and-language navigation in continuous environments (VLN-CE), an agent follows a natural-language instruction I I through a continuous 3D environment ( Krantz et al., 2020 ) . At time t t , it receives an egocentric observation o t o_{t} and acts from the navigation history H t = ( o 0 , a 0 , … , a t − 1 , o t ) . H_{t}=(o_{0},a_{0},\ldots,a_{t-1},o_{t}). (1) A navigation policy assigns a conditional distribution π θ ​ ( a t ∣ I , H t ) \pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid I,H_{t}) over its next one or few actions. A full episode ends when the agent emits Stop or reaches the maximum steps, and success means stopping near the destination. We study the widely used four-action interface 𝒜 = { Forward , Left , Right , Stop } , \mathcal{A}=\{\textsc{Forward},\textsc{Left},\textsc{Right},\textsc{Stop}\}, (2) adopted by low-level VLN-CE agents Krantz et al. (2020) and recent navigation VLAs ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Wei et al., 2025 ; Zeng et al., 2026 ; Zuo et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026a ) . Forward advances the agent by a fixed distance, while Left and Right rotate it by a fixed angular increment. This finite action vocabulary provides a common behavioural interface and, for models that expose action logits, permits exact likelihood evaluation of a fixed action sequence.

sections.heading: 3.2 Local Route-Fork Diagnosis
sections.text: Within each source pair, a local diagnostic context consists of a valid history H h H_{h} ending at a nonterminal route fork v v and its completed instruction prefix P h P_{h} , where h ∈ { A , B } h\in\{A,B\} identifies the source route (Figure 2 (a)). Each remaining suffix S s S_{s} , with s ∈ { A , B } s\in\{A,B\} , specifies one outgoing branch. The full input instruction is I h , s = P h + S s I_{h,s}=P_{h}+S_{s} , and an evaluation condition consists of H h H_{h} and I h , s I_{h,s} . From the state reached by H h H_{h} , the reference action sequence for either executable branch g ∈ { A , B } g\in\{A,B\} is G h , g = ( a 1 h , g , … , a K h , g h , g ) , K h , g ≤ K . G_{h,g}=(a^{h,g}_{1},\ldots,a^{h,g}_{K_{h,g}}),\quad K_{h,g}\leq K. (3) The diagnostic horizon K K limits its length, and Stop ends the sequence. For each context ( H h , P h ) (H_{h},P_{h}) , NavBind compares I h , A I_{h,A} and I h , B I_{h,B} , as in a horizontal comparison in Figure 2 (b). Both conditions start from exactly the same pose, current observation, and observation-action history. Instruction-action binding requires the model to assign higher probability to the actions required by the suffix. Section 4 describes how route geometry and fine-grained language annotations yield these matched conditions.

sections.heading: 4.1 Route-Aligned Source Pairs
sections.text: We construct source pairs from English R2R-CE and RxR-CE routes and instructions ( Anderson et al., 2018 ; Ku et al., 2020 ; Krantz et al., 2020 ) . For R2R and English RxR, we use released fine-grained annotations from FGR2R ( Hong et al., 2020 ) and Landmark-RxR ( He et al., 2021 ) , respectively. These annotations divide full instructions into shorter text segments, called sub-instructions , and align each segment with the part of the trajectory it describes. We first identify route pairs with the structure shown in Figure 2 (a): two routes in the same scene share a directed segment from u u to the fork v v , then take different outgoing edges at v v . The routes may differ before u u . Both branches beyond v v must be executable and nonterminal. We require a sufficiently long shared segment u → v u\!\to\!v to align the two routes’ positions and orientations at v v . Sharing v v alone leaves arrival orientation unconstrained, which can change the interpretation of instructions such as “turn left.” For each source route h h in a candidate pair, we use the sub-instruction annotations to place the language boundary at v v . An edge-exact boundary requires the preceding subpath to end at v v and the next subpath to start at v v with its first edge entering branch h h . We recover the corresponding original-text offsets by monotonic matching with case, spacing, and punctuation normalized. Cutting at the start of that next sub-instruction yields I h , h = P h + S h I_{h,h}=P_{h}+S_{h} : the prefix P h P_{h} covers the full route up to v v , including any portion before u u , and the suffix S h S_{h} retains the remaining instruction. Both spans preserve their original wording. Selection uses route annotations alone. Repeated physical forks are deduplicated. For each retained pair, expert replay of route h h from its source start to v v yields a history H h H_{h} paired with its completed prefix P h P_{h} . From each state at v v , we construct both local branch targets G h , A G_{h,A} and G h , B G_{h,B} . The resulting history-prefix pairs form the fixed row contexts in Figure 2 (b).

sections.heading: Suffix intervention.
sections.text: Within each row, the diagonal instruction I h , h I_{h,h} retains the source text, and the off-diagonal instruction substitutes the other route’s suffix. Evaluating I h , A I_{h,A} and I h , B I_{h,B} from the same replay history and fork state implements the primary fixed-context comparison defined in Section 3.2 .

sections.heading: Matched prefix intervention.
sections.text: Across rows, the supplementary comparison between ( H A , I A , s ) (H_{A},I_{A,s}) and ( H B , I B , s ) (H_{B},I_{B,s}) holds the suffix fixed while jointly changing the history and its source prefix. It compares the model’s response to the same branch beyond v v across the two source-matched contexts. Each source pair initially yields two candidate contexts and four conditions, linked by a source-pair identifier. We retain contexts whose two reference sequences differ within four actions at every evaluated native action scale. The resulting NavBind set contains 3,252 contexts from 1,648 source pairs, shared by all models.

sections.heading: 5 Diagnosing Instruction-Action Binding
sections.text: Figure 3: Action likelihood and visual attribution. (a) Conditional action-token probabilities for each fixed reference under the two suffixes. Arrows denote left, forward, and right actions. (b) Full attention × \times gradient heatmaps for each suffix’s corresponding reference. Warmer colors indicate higher attribution on a shared scale. IoU uses the original top-25% masks. Given the matched conditions constructed in Section 4 , we analyze instruction-action binding from three complementary perspectives. We first measure whether an intervention changes the generated local action sequence. We then measure how it changes the likelihood and action distribution of a fixed reference target. Finally, we examine how visual attention and attribution change across conditions. Likelihood comparisons keep the target fixed, while gradient-based attribution follows each instruction’s corresponding GT. Figure 3 illustrates these comparisons on one navigation context.

sections.heading: 6.1 Data and Models
sections.text: We evaluate Uni-NaVid ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) , StreamVLN ( Wei et al., 2025 ) , JanusVLN ( Zeng et al., 2026 ) , and FutureNav ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) on the same 3,252 NavBind contexts constructed in Section 4 , using released checkpoints.

sections.heading: 6.2 Evaluation Protocol
sections.text: We use a four-action horizon ( K = 4 K=4 ) and each model’s native action increments. Uni-NaVid and StreamVLN generate action chunks under fixed observations, while JanusVLN and FutureNav execute each predicted action before the next decision. We retain native decoding: Uni-NaVid uses sampling and StreamVLN uses greedy decoding.

sections.heading: 7.1 Main Results
sections.text: In Table 1 , Uni-NaVid has the highest reported RxR-CE val-unseen SR. However, StreamVLN has the highest d ¯ \bar{d} and KL values. Uni-NaVid’s Both+ is 29.15%, only 4.15 percentage points above a 25% reference. This reference assumes that the two likelihood gains are independent and each has a 50% chance of being positive. StreamVLN and FutureNav have nearly identical reported SR (54.4% and 54.5%), yet StreamVLN has higher d ¯ \bar{d} (0.8360 versus 0.4411), Both+ (80.38% versus 70.60%), and KL (0.8233 versus 0.6208). Thus, higher navigation success does not necessarily mean that changing the instruction has a larger effect on action probabilities. JanusVLN and FutureNav change their action sequences more often than StreamVLN (lower Same seq.), but show smaller likelihood gains for the instructed action sequences (lower d ¯ \bar{d} ). Their attention and attribution heatmaps also highlight more similar visual regions across instructions (higher IoU). One possible explanation is that these models rely on similar visual cues without clearly distinguishing the instructed branch, leaving them less confident about which action to take. Small probability shifts could then be enough to change the selected action.

sections.heading: 7.6 Larger Original-Pairing Advantages on Training Sources

sections.heading: 8 Conclusion
sections.text: NavBind diagnoses instruction-action binding through route-fork interventions under fixed navigation contexts, combining generated behavior, fixed-target likelihoods, and visual attention and attribution. Across 3,252 shared contexts, higher reported navigation success does not always mean more frequent action changes or larger shifts in action probabilities. These findings support evaluating how language affects local decisions alongside episode-level navigation success.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Recombining source instructions may introduce ambiguity or unnatural transitions at the segment boundaries. The four-action window captures local instruction responses, while later responses and error recovery remain outside the evaluation horizon. Model-native action increments also give this window different physical extents across models. Visual IoU quantifies spatial changes in attention and attribution, without establishing whether the selected regions are relevant to the instructed branch or causally determine the action.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.29203v1 [cs.RO] 21 Oct 2026 NavBind : Diagnosing Instruction-Action Binding at Route Forks in Navigation VLAs Josh Qixuan Sun Affiliation: University of Waterloo Xiaoying Xing Affiliation: Northwest University Yurun Chen Affiliation: Eastern Institute of Technology Huaiyuan Weng Affiliation: University of Waterloo Wentao Zhu Affiliation: Eastern Institute of Technology Mark Crowley Affiliation: University of Waterloo Abstract Vision-language-action (VLA) navigation models translate visual observations and instructions into actions. Navigation success assesses whether an agent reaches the goal. However, reaching the goal successfully does not establish whether the model genuinely follows the instructions or relies on visual cues or navigation history. We introduce NavBind to diagnose instruction-action binding: whether changing the instruction influences the probabilistic distribution of the actions, with the navigation context fixed. We construct 3,252 route-fork contexts by recombining route-aligned instruction segments from R2R-CE and RxR-CE. Each context pairs full instructions that share the description of the route already traveled but specify different branches. Both are evaluated under the same agent state and navigation history. We compare generated local action sequences, the likelihoods of fixed reference action sequences under both instructions, and changes in visual attention and attribution. Across the evaluated models, higher reported navigation success does not imply that the model more faithfully follows the instructions. 1 Introduction Figure 1: Does the action follow the instruction? NavBind pairs one fixed navigation history H H with two full instructions P + S A P+S_{A} and P + S B P+S_{B} . The shared prefix P P describes the completed route, and the remaining suffixes S A S_{A} and S B S_{B} specify different executable branches. This example contrasts turning left with going up the stairs. We jointly examine generated action-sequence changes, fixed-target action likelihood, visual attention, and attribution for each instruction’s corresponding reference actions. In vision-and-language navigation in continuous environments (VLN-CE) ( Krantz et al., 2020 ) , vision-language-action (VLA) models ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) map visual observations and instructions to actions. Success rate measures whether an agent reaches the goal but does not establish whether it follows the instruction. Route-fidelity metrics ( Jain et al., 2019 ) assess the similarity between the generated trajectory and the ground-truth trajectory, providing an indirect measure of instruction following. However, these metrics still cannot establish whether the model genuinely follows the instructions , as it may instead rely on visual cues or navigation history alone. Language interventions, i.e., changing the language instruction and observing how the local actions or navigation performance change, provide a more direct test of language dependence. NavTrust ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) and Contrast Sets ( Anwar et al., 2025 ) rephrase instructions and assess changes in navigation performance. However, these tests keep the intended navigation behaviour unchanged. R2RIE-CE ( Taioli et al., 2024 ) modifies instructions by injecting direction, object, and room errors. However, it neither ensures that the modified instructions describe feasible routes nor provides reference actions corresponding to them. Without matching reference trajectories for the modified instructions, a behavioural change alone does not show that the model followed them. We therefore ask not merely whether the model’s behaviour changes, but whether changing the instruction to describe another feasible route makes the model more likely to choose the corresponding actions . We keep the agent’s state, navigation history, and completed instruction prefix fixed. In Figure 1 , both turning left and continuing up the stairs are feasible, and the remaining instruction specifies which branch to take. We use instruction-action binding to describe the requirement that the model assigns higher probability to the actions required by the instruction. We introduce NavBind , a controlled diagnostic built through cross-route recombination of route-instruction examples drawn from R2R-CE and RxR-CE. Using fine-grained route-language alignments, we retain one example’s completed instruction prefix and combine it with either its original suffix or a compatible suffix from another route. The resulting full-instruction pairs specify different executable branches under the same replayed history and agent state, yielding 3,252 contexts with reference action sequences for both branches. Within each fixed context, we first ask: does changing the instruction change the action sequence the model generates? We then ask: does the model assign higher probability to the actions for a branch when instructed to take that branch rather than the other? We test this by comparing the likelihood of each reference action sequence under the two instructions. This comparison can reveal changes in action preference even when the generated sequence stays the same. Finally, we examine the visual response: do attention heatmaps and gradient-based attribution heatmaps highlight different image regions under the two instructions? We evaluate four navigation VLAs on NavBind : Uni-NaVid ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) , StreamVLN ( Wei et al., 2025 ) , JanusVLN ( Zeng et al., 2026 ) , and FutureNav ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) . We find that higher reported navigation success does not imply that the model more faithfully follows the instructions. (Table 1 ). It also shows that models respond more strongly when the instructions contrast opposite turns than when they contrast forward movement with a turn. Our contributions are: • We construct NavBind by recombining instruction segments across routes into full instructions for two feasible branches. Each pair preserves the agent state, history, and completed instruction prefix, and provides reference action sequences for both branches. • We diagnose instruction-action binding using generated sequences to measure output changes, fixed-target likelihoods to assess preferences for the instructed actions, and attention and gradient-based attribution heatmaps to track spatial changes. • We show that higher reported navigation success does not imply that the model more faithfully follows the instructions. This supports evaluating how language affects local decisions alongside navigation success. 2 Related Work 2.1 Language Diagnostics in VLN Instruction fidelity beyond success. Goal completion can obscure whether an agent followed the described route. Stay on the Path introduced CLS and longer R4R routes ( Jain et al., 2019 ) , while LAW extended language-aligned supervision and evaluation to VLN-CE ( Raychaudhuri et al., 2021 ) . Modality ablations further showed that R2R agents could rely strongly on graph structure ( Hu et al., 2019 ) . These works motivate language-specific evaluation through task metrics, supervision, and modality ablations. Language interventions in VLN. Early diagnostics mask object, direction, and numerical cues ( Zhu et al., 2022 ) and swap directional tokens ( Hahn et al., 2023 ) . Skill-focused evaluations append atomic instructions to truncated RxR episodes ( Yang et al., 2023 ) and construct human-refined atomic instructions, including same-start left/right pairs ( Wang et al., 2024 ) . These studies evaluate agents on discrete navigation graphs and their action tests cannot be directly applied to navigation VLAs that execute low-level actions. In VLN-CE, NavTrust evaluates whether agents maintain navigation performance under instruction corruption and stylistic variation ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) . Contrast Sets tests instruction rephrasing with unchanged navigation goals on a physical robot ( Anwar et al., 2025 ) . However, these tests keep the intended navigation behaviour unchanged. R2RIE-CE injects direction, object, and room errors into instructions to study error detection and localization ( Taioli et al., 2024 ) . The modified instructions are not paired with matching reference trajectories. However, it neither ensures that the modified instructions describe feasible routes nor provides reference actions corresponding to them. Without matching reference trajectories for the modified instructions, a behavioural change alone does not show that the model followed them. CAST pairs generated alternative instructions with short action branches for counterfactual training ( Glossop et al., 2026 ) , but the intended action behaviour only include a short horizon rather than a long horizon. NavBind constructs full-instruction pairs for long-horizon navigation by recombining original route-aligned instruction spans across source routes. The pairs specify different executable branches under the same agent state, navigation history, and completed instruction prefix. Scoring both reference action sequences under both instructions tests whether the model’s local action preferences shift toward the instructed branch. 2.2 Language-Action Coupling in VLAs Recent work examines whether language and other multimodal signals influence VLA action generation. VLA-Trace connects representation similarity, attention-path knockouts, and rollout-level behavioural probes ( Shi et al., 2026 ) , while Häon et al. (2025) identify semantic activation directions and intervene on them to steer actions. Zhang et al. (2026b) diagnose linguistic blindness in manipulation VLAs using contradictory instructions and recalibrate attention at inference time, while Zhan et al. (2026) study robustness to linguistic perturbations and strengthen language guidance through residual steering. These studies establish that language and internal pathways can affect VLA actions, but their evaluations center on manipulation and often combine diagnosis with model modification. NavBind tests instruction-action binding in frozen navigation VLAs: two valid route instructions share the same history but specify different executable branches. We align behaviour with fixed-target likelihood and visual attribution. 3 Problem Setting 3.1 VLN-CE In vision-and-language navigation in continuous environments (VLN-CE), an agent follows a natural-language instruction I I through a continuous 3D environment ( Krantz et al., 2020 ) . At time t t , it receives an egocentric observation o t o_{t} and acts from the navigation history H t = ( o 0 , a 0 , … , a t − 1 , o t ) . H_{t}=(o_{0},a_{0},\ldots,a_{t-1},o_{t}). (1) A navigation policy assigns a conditional distribution π θ ​ ( a t ∣ I , H t ) \pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid I,H_{t}) over its next one or few actions. A full episode ends when the agent emits Stop or reaches the maximum steps, and success means stopping near the destination. We study the widely used four-action interface 𝒜 = { Forward , Left , Right , Stop } , \mathcal{A}=\{\textsc{Forward},\textsc{Left},\textsc{Right},\textsc{Stop}\}, (2) adopted by low-level VLN-CE agents Krantz et al. (2020) and recent navigation VLAs ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Wei et al., 2025 ; Zeng et al., 2026 ; Zuo et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026a ) . Forward advances the agent by a fixed distance, while Left and Right rotate it by a fixed angular increment. This finite action vocabulary provides a common behavioural interface and, for models that expose action logits, permits exact likelihood evaluation of a fixed action sequence. 3.2 Local Route-Fork Diagnosis Within each source pair, a local diagnostic context consists of a valid history H h H_{h} ending at a nonterminal route fork v v and its completed instruction prefix P h P_{h} , where h ∈ { A , B } h\in\{A,B\} identifies the source route (Figure 2 (a)). Instruction-action binding requires the model to assign higher probability to the actions required by the suffix. (a) Original routes A/B (blue/orange) share a directed segment from u u to fork v v , then diverge. Dashed paths are traversed, and solid paths remain. Each full instruction I h , h = P h + S h I_{h,h}=P_{h}+S_{h} splits at v v into completed prefix P h P_{h} and remaining suffix S h S_{h} . (b) Horizontal comparisons change only the suffix. Vertical comparisons change history and prefix together with the suffix fixed. 4.1 Route-Aligned Source Pairs We construct source pairs from English R2R-CE and RxR-CE routes and instructions ( Anderson et al., 2018 ; Ku et al., 2020 ; Krantz et al., 2020 ) . For R2R and English RxR, we use released fine-grained annotations from FGR2R ( Hong et al., 2020 ) and Landmark-RxR ( He et al., 2021 ) , respectively. These annotations divide full instructions into shorter text segments, called sub-instructions , and align each segment with the part of the trajectory it describes. We first identify route pairs with the structure shown in Figure 2 (a): two routes in the same scene share a directed segment from u u to the fork v v , then take different outgoing edges at v v . The routes may differ before u u . Both branches beyond v v must be executable and nonterminal. We require a sufficiently long shared segment u → v u\!\to\!v to align the two routes’ positions and orientations at v v . Sharing v v alone leaves arrival orientation unconstrained, which can change the interpretation of instructions such as “turn left.” For each source route h h in a candidate pair, we use the sub-instruction annotations to place the language boundary at v v . An edge-exact boundary requires the preceding subpath to end at v v and the next subpath to start at v v with its first edge entering branch h h . We recover the corresponding original-text offsets by monotonic matching with case, spacing, and punctuation normalized. Cutting at the start of that next sub-instruction yields I h , h = P h + S h I_{h,h}=P_{h}+S_{h} : the prefix P h P_{h} covers the full route up to v v , including any portion before u u , and the suffix S h S_{h} retains the remaining instruction. Both spans preserve their original wording. Selection uses route annotations alone. Repeated physical forks are deduplicated. For each retained pair, expert replay of route h h from its source start to v v yields a history H h H_{h} paired with its completed prefix P h P_{h} . From each state at v v , we construct both local branch targets G h , A G_{h,A} and G h , B G_{h,B} . The resulting history-prefix pairs form the fixed row contexts in Figure 2 (b). 4.2 Matched Interventions Figure 2 (b) crosses each context ( H h , P h ) (H_{h},P_{h}) with both suffixes. Each cell gives the instruction I h , s I_{h,s} , evaluated with the history H h H_{h} in its row. Suffix intervention. Within each row, the diagonal instruction I h , h I_{h,h} retains the source text, and the off-diagonal instruction substitutes the other route’s suffix. Evaluating I h , A I_{h,A} and I h , B I_{h,B} from the same replay history and fork state implements the primary fixed-context comparison defined in Section 3.2 . Matched prefix intervention. Across rows, the supplementary comparison between ( H A , I A , s ) (H_{A},I_{A,s}) and ( H B , I B , s ) (H_{B},I_{B,s}) holds the suffix fixed while jointly changing the history and its source prefix. It compares the model’s response to the same branch beyond v v across the two source-matched contexts. Each source pair initially yields two candidate contexts and four conditions, linked by a source-pair identifier. We retain contexts whose two reference sequences differ within four actions at every evaluated native action scale. The resulting NavBind set contains 3,252 contexts from 1,648 source pairs, shared by all models. 5 Diagnosing Instruction-Action Binding Figure 3: Action likelihood and visual attribution. (a) Conditional action-token probabilities for each fixed reference under the two suffixes. Arrows denote left, forward, and right actions. (b) Full attention × \times gradient heatmaps for each suffix’s corresponding reference. Warmer colors indicate higher attribution on a shared scale. IoU uses the original top-25% masks. Given the matched conditions constructed in Section 4 , we analyze instruction-action binding from three complementary perspectives. We first measure whether an intervention changes the generated local action sequence. We then measure how it changes the likelihood and action distribution of a fixed reference target. Finally, we examine how visual attention and attribution change across conditions. Likelihood comparisons keep the target fixed, while gradient-based attribution follows each instruction’s corresponding GT. Figure 3 illustrates these comparisons on one navigation context. 5.1 Generated Action Sequences For each context ( H h , P h ) (H_{h},P_{h}) , we generate local action sequences under I h , A I_{h,A} and I h , B I_{h,B} using native inference without teacher forcing. We report the percentage of contexts whose sequences match exactly in action symbols, order, and length within horizon K K as Same sequence (Same seq.). 5.2 Fixed-Target Action Likelihood Discrete generation can remain unchanged even when model’s action distribution changes. We therefore measure changes in the likelihood of fixed reference action sequences. Across 3,252 shared contexts, higher reported navigation success does not always mean more frequent action changes or larger shifts in action probabilities. These findings support evaluating how language affects local decisions alongside episode-level navigation success. Limitations Recombining source instructions may introduce ambiguity or unnatural transitions at the segment boundaries. The four-action window captures local instruction responses, while later responses and error recovery remain outside the evaluation horizon. Model-native action increments also give this window different physical extents across models. Visual IoU quantifies spatial changes in attention and attribution, without establishing whether the selected regions are relevant to the instructed branch or causally determine the action.
